g10-history-uh9-t1.overview: Indigenous knowledge is the local knowledge that Ethiopian communities have used for generations to earn a living and to organise their social, economic and spiritual lives. This lesson defines it, lists the forms it takes, and explains its characteristics and its role in the country's development.
objectives: Define indigenous knowledge and explain why it is called local knowledge
List the main forms in which indigenous knowledge appears
Explain the characteristics of indigenous knowledge
Assess the role of indigenous knowledge in overall development
Give concrete examples of indigenous knowledge from Ethiopian communities
g10-history-uh9-t1.simple: Indigenous knowledge is the knowledge that helps a society decide which activities fit its way of life. It is the knowledge local people use to earn a living in their own setting, so it is often called local knowledge. It is passed from generation to generation by oral tradition and by practice. Indigenous knowledge shapes people's worldviews and guides their social, economic, political and spiritual survival. It appears as indigenous laws and rituals, local systems for classifying plants, animals, soils, water, air and weather, local counting and measuring methods, farming and crop systems, indigenous medicine and pest management. It is simple, practical and expressed in local languages. It gives local solutions, conserves resources and forms a basic and rich ground for modern development.
g10-history-uh9-t1.detailed:
What indigenous knowledge is. Indigenous knowledge is the knowledge that assists society in making judgments regarding activities that are compatible with their way of life. It is the knowledge that locals utilise to earn a living in a certain setting, and it is often known as local knowledge. It is what indigenous people have passed down from generation to generation through oral tradition and practice. It shapes people's worldviews and gives guidance for their social, economic, political and spiritual survival.

The forms it takes. Indigenous knowledge can take many forms. These include indigenous laws and rituals; local classification and quantification systems for plants, animals, soils, water, air and weather; indigenous methods of counting and quantifying; and learning systems such as indigenous educational methods, indigenous agricultural farming and crop systems, indigenous medicine and pest management systems.

Its role in overall development. Indigenous knowledge provides problem-solving strategies for local communities and represents an important component of global knowledge on development issues. Learning from it improves understanding of local conditions, because indigenous people can provide valuable input about the local environment and how to manage natural resources effectively. Indigenous knowledge systems and technologies have been proven to be socially desired, economically viable and sustainable, posing little danger to rural farmers and producers and, most importantly, conserving resources. Learning from indigenous knowledge improves understanding of agriculture, healthcare, food security, education and natural resource management, and preserving it contributes to cultural and political self-reliance.

Simple and practical. Indigenous knowledge is simple and practical. It links the survival of every human being to the wholeness of nature and its elements that support life. It provides the concrete situations of communities regarding the environment and offers practical solutions to the problems of the people. It deals with simple but applied education, economics, politics, religion, sciences and technologies of indigenous societies, and it provides a basic and rich ground for the development of modern society.

Developed over a long period. Indigenous knowledge developed over a long period. Its patterns are based upon local knowledge systems, and it is expressed in local languages. In many cases this knowledge has been passed from generation to generation orally, and some forms of it are expressed through stories, legends, folklore, rituals, songs and even laws.

Why it matters today. Some people wrongly believe that only modern science counts as real knowledge. The textbook argues the opposite: indigenous knowledge is part of global knowledge on development, it conserves resources, and it is socially desired, economically viable and sustainable. Ethiopia's own development therefore depends partly on learning from, recording and preserving the knowledge of its farmers, healers and elders alongside modern science.

Another name for indigenous knowledge, because it is generated and used by people in a particular locality and culture.
The passing of knowledge, laws and stories from generation to generation by word of mouth and by practice rather than in writing.
Local knowledge and practice that a community uses in healing; it is listed among the forms of indigenous knowledge.
An indigenous crop-protection practice named in the textbook among the forms of indigenous knowledge.
A prescribed set of symbolic actions performed on religious or social occasions; one of the forms through which indigenous knowledge is expressed.
Able to continue over time without destroying the resources it depends on; the textbook says indigenous knowledge systems are socially desired, economically viable and sustainable.

workedExamples.problem: Using the textbook definition, explain why indigenous knowledge is called local knowledge and how it is transmitted.
workedExamples.given: Indigenous knowledge is the knowledge that assists society in making judgments about activities compatible with its way of life; it is the knowledge locals utilise to earn a living in a certain setting; it is passed down through oral tradition and practice.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: definition and transmission of indigenous knowledge.
workedExamples.substitution: The knowledge is tied to one particular place and people, and it is handed down by word of mouth and by practice rather than in written textbooks.
workedExamples.calculation: Because locals use it to live in a certain setting it is local knowledge; because it is handed down by speech and practice it travels through oral tradition.
workedExamples.answer: It is called local knowledge because locals use it in a particular setting, and it is transmitted from generation to generation through oral tradition and practice.

workedExamples.problem: Identify the role of indigenous knowledge in the development of Ethiopian agriculture.
workedExamples.given: Indigenous knowledge systems and technologies are socially desired, economically viable and sustainable; they pose little danger to rural farmers and conserve resources; learning from them improves agriculture, healthcare, food security, education and natural resource management.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: the role of indigenous knowledge for overall development.
workedExamples.substitution: In farming this means local crop systems, local classification of soils, water and weather, and indigenous pest management.
workedExamples.calculation: These practices raise production while conserving resources and carrying little danger for farmers, so they support development that lasts.
workedExamples.answer: Indigenous knowledge supplies locally proven, low-risk, resource-conserving practices that improve farm production and food security.

workedExamples.problem: A student claims that indigenous knowledge is unscientific and useless. Evaluate this claim using the textbook characteristics.
workedExamples.given: Characteristics: indigenous knowledge is simple and practical; it deals with applied education, economics, politics, religion, sciences and technologies of indigenous societies; it developed over a long period and is expressed through stories, legends, folklore, rituals, songs and laws.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: characteristics of indigenous knowledge.
workedExamples.substitution: Practical farming, healing, counting and weather methods are applied science and technology built up over a long period.
workedExamples.calculation: Since the knowledge is practical, applied and long-tested, the claim that it is useless contradicts the textbook; what it lacks is written form, not usefulness.
workedExamples.answer: The claim is false: indigenous knowledge is simple, practical and long-tested, and it provides basic and rich ground for modern development.

commonMistakes: Thinking indigenous knowledge is the same thing as superstition or ignorance.
Believing that only written, modern science counts as real knowledge.
Assuming indigenous knowledge belongs only to the past and has no role in development today.
Treating all indigenous knowledge as identical in every Ethiopian community.
Forgetting that indigenous knowledge is transmitted mainly by oral tradition and practice, not in books.
Ignoring the fact that indigenous technologies are sustainable and conserve natural resources.

Using local soil and water classification to plan a school garden or tree-planting project.
Asking traditional healers and health workers to explain the same illness so that both kinds of knowledge are understood.
Preserving local proverbs, songs and stories that carry community knowledge.
Combining indigenous crop systems with modern advice on a family farm.
Documenting the counting and measuring systems used in a local market.
g10-history-uh9-t1.summary: Indigenous knowledge, also called local knowledge, is the knowledge a society uses to judge which activities fit its way of life and to earn a living in its own setting. It is passed from generation to generation through oral tradition and practice, and it appears in laws, rituals, local classification and counting systems, farming, medicine and pest management. It is simple, practical, long-tested and expressed in local languages, and it supports overall development in agriculture, health, food security, education and natural resource management.

g10-history-uh9-t2.overview: Ethiopia has age-old, culturally deep-rooted systems of governance and dispute resolution that differ from region to region. This lesson examines the Mada'a and Dagu of the Afar, the Gadaa, jaarsummaa, gumaa and Siinqee of the Oromo, the Shimgelina of the Amhara, and the Luwa and Seera systems of other peoples.
objectives: Identify indigenous conflict resolution methods used in Ethiopia
Describe the Mada'a and Dagu systems of the Afar people
Explain the Gadaa system and the Oromo institutions of jaarsummaa, gumaa and Siinqee
Compare the Shimgelina of the Amhara with the jaarsummaa of the Oromo
Assess the roles of elders and of the Luwa and Seera systems in community life
g10-history-uh9-t2.simple: In Ethiopia, indigenous knowledge appears as management strategies, decision-making procedures, dispute resolution practices, indigenous laws and rights. Indigenous conflict resolution is one of the most popular ways of settling disputes. It is informal and works through arbitration and mediation. Local leaders, chiefs, religious leaders, healers and elders lead the process because they know local customs, traditions and history. The aim is a solution based on the recognised customs and morality of the society, and it helps restore good relations between the parties. Examples include the Mada'a and Dagu of the Afar, the Gadaa, jaarsummaa, gumaa and Siinqee of the Oromo, the Shimgelina of the Amhara, and the Luwa and Seera systems of the Sidama, Kambata and Hadiya.
g10-history-uh9-t2.detailed:
Indigenous knowledge in practice and the role of elders. Indigenous knowledge is manifested in numerous ways, such as management strategies, decision-making procedures, dispute resolution practices, indigenous laws and rights. In Ethiopia, indigenous conflict resolution is one of the most popular techniques of conflict settlement. It is an informal way of resolving conflicts, an old collection of techniques found in all communities, and it works through arbitration and mediation. Its main aim is to reach a solution based on the recognised customs and morality of the society, and it helps to restore a good relationship among the conflicting parties. Local leaders, chiefs, religious leaders, healers and elders lead the process, and they are respected for their extensive understanding of local customs, traditions, history and the relationships of the contending parties. Their expertise, their ability to understand symbols of reconciliation, their oratory abilities and their social capital enable them to negotiate a settlement.

Mada'a and Dagu of the Afar. The Afar are a predominantly pastoral community who inhabit the northeastern part of Ethiopia. Their indigenous mechanism of conflict resolution is known as Mada'a, an unwritten law transmitted orally from generation to generation. Elders of the Mada'a, who do not represent members in disputes, are selected from different clans, and their decisions are effective because of the tradition of forgiveness, respect for elders and the transfer of resources as compensation. Because of their pastoral way of life the Afar also have a unique information exchange system called Dagu, an age-old system of information management that involves passing and receiving information or news about what two or more individuals have seen or heard. Dagu serves virtually all members of society equally, regardless of social status, and it carries news of newcomers, the conditions of water holes and grazing lands, missing camels and caravans, weddings and funerals, new alliances and betrayals, the latest battles and the condition of the trail ahead.

Gadaa and the Oromo institutions. Gadaa is the indigenous democratic system of governance of the Oromo. In it the people are grouped and organised into five Gadaa classes that succeed each other every eight years in assuming economic, political, military and social responsibilities. The foundation of the system is rooted in the customary Oromo institutions of aadaa (custom or tradition), seera (laws), safuu, a moral category that prescribes what human actions and behaviours ought to be and is the Oromo concept of ethics, and heera (justice). These institutions form indigenous systems of knowledge, include the rules and regulations that determine access to natural resources, and serve as conflict-resolution institutions able to tackle the interlinked problems of environment, welfare and conflict.

Jaarsummaa, araara and gumaa. In most Ethiopian traditions, community elders are key decision-makers and conflict mediators. The institution of araara is reconciliation, and the process of reconciliation between conflicting individuals or groups by a group of jaarsaas is jaarsummaa; jaarsa is the Oromo version of elder. The decision of the elders emphasises the need for cooperation and a win-win solution instead of unconstructive competition that produces a win-lose result. An Oromo proverb expresses this ideal: Akka Haroon hin gognee akka raachi hin dune, meaning for the lake not to dry, for the frogs not to die. Gumaa is the widely practised indigenous way of resolving conflicts relating to homicide or murder; it is the blood money paid to the slain person's family or the payment made to seriously injured individuals. Decisions in the gumaa system are made after close examination of data obtained from witnesses, the conflicting parties express repentance, and the system also has its own way of secretly investigating crimes committed against human life or property.

Siinqee of Oromo women. Siinqee (Siiqee) is the instrument through which women's rights are duly respected among the Oromo. It is a stick (ulee) symbolising a socially sanctioned set of rights exercised by women, and it is a special stick that a woman who gets legally married receives on her wedding day. Siinqee is also an institution, a women's organisation that excludes men and has both religious and political functions. Women use it to protect their property rights, to assert control over sexuality and fertility, to protect their social rights and to maintain religious and moral authority. Whenever a woman's right has been violated, the women ululate to notify one another, every woman is obliged to respond, and they move to the place carrying their Siinqee and go to the Gada Council singing a song that announces the specific activities that led to the breach of their rights. There they are welcomed respectfully and invited to speak out, after which the person accused of wrongdoing is brought to justice.

Shimgelina of the Amhara. Among the Amhara people the main indigenous conflict resolution mechanism is Shimgelina, which is comparable to the jaarsuumma of the Oromo. In it, five shimageles (elders) are appointed by the disputing parties themselves on the basis of their choice. They are recognised as solution makers because they have the power to make binding decisions and to impose solutions, and they can sanction social measures if one party fails to comply with the ruling or agreement. Shimegilena is preferable because of its accessibility, low cost and trust, and in most cases a priest of the local church serves as chairman to make the system more acceptable to society. The disputants take part in ceremonies celebrating the resolution, such as exchanging assets, prayers and sacrifice, jumping over rifles, drinking and eating jointly, and playing and dancing.

Sidama Luwa and Seera; Kambata and Hadiya Seera. The Sidama Luwa system is an age-related institution performing ritual, cultural and political roles, administered by an age grade system in which each grade rotates every eight years. There are five rotating age grades: Darara, Fullassa, Hirobora, Wawassa and Mogissa. Its two objectives are the recruitment and training of able-bodied men for the defence of the nation and the development of potential elders who will replace the current elders (Cimeeyye). The Sidama Seera system is divided into two, the broad concept of Seera as a social constitution that governs Sidama social life on the basis of the moral code of halale, the ultimate truth, which provides the basis for distinguishing good from evil. In Kambata and Hadiya culture, Seera is the basis for political administration, social involvement and dispute resolution; it governs the interactions of people, clans and territorial groups, and its goals are peace, correction and reintegration, overseen by wise and patient village elders with wide-ranging knowledge of justice and peace.

keyTerms.def: The indigenous conflict resolution mechanism of the predominantly pastoral Afar people of northeastern Ethiopia, an unwritten law transmitted orally from generation to generation.
The age-old indigenous information exchange network of the Afar, which passes and receives news about what two or more individuals have seen or heard and serves all members equally.
The indigenous democratic system of governance of the Oromo, in which five Gadaa classes succeed each other every eight years in assuming economic, political, military and social responsibilities.
The Oromo process of reconciliation between conflicting individuals or groups by a group of jaarsaas (elders), aimed at a win-win solution.
The widely practised indigenous way of resolving conflicts relating to homicide or murder; the blood money paid to the slain person's family or to seriously injured individuals.
A stick (ulee) and an institution of Oromo women that symbolises socially sanctioned rights and helps to protect women's rights and resolve conflicts.
The main indigenous conflict resolution mechanism of the Amhara, in which five shimageles appointed by the disputing parties make binding decisions.
A code of behaviour or social constitution that governs community life, used by the Sidama on the basis of halale and by the Kambata and Hadiya as the basis of administration and dispute resolution.

workedExamples.problem: The Afar community needs to spread news about missing camels, water holes and grazing land across a wide desert. Which indigenous system does this, and why is it suited to a pastoral way of life?
workedExamples.given: The Afar are a predominantly pastoral community in the northeastern part of Ethiopia and their information exchange system is called Dagu.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: the function of an indigenous knowledge system within its environment.
workedExamples.substitution: Pastoralists move constantly, so they need fast, wide-reaching news about water, grazing land and animals.
workedExamples.calculation: Dagu is an age-old system of information management that passes and receives news about what two or more people have seen or heard, and it serves all members almost equally regardless of social status.
workedExamples.answer: Dagu, the Afar information exchange system, because it carries environmental and animal news to all members of a mobile pastoral society.

workedExamples.problem: Compare jaarsummaa of the Oromo and Shimgelina of the Amhara as indigenous conflict resolution mechanisms.
workedExamples.given: Jaarsummaa is reconciliation by a group of jaarsaas (elders); Shimgelina uses five shimageles appointed by the disputing parties themselves, who can make binding decisions and sanction non-compliance, and a local priest often serves as chairman.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: comparison of indigenous dispute resolution through arbitration and mediation.
workedExamples.substitution: Both aim at a solution based on recognised customs and morality that restores good relations among the parties.
workedExamples.calculation: Both are informal and elder-led; Shimgelina stands out because five elders are chosen by the parties and have power to sanction, while jaarsummaa stands out for its ideal of a win-win outcome expressed in the proverb about the lake and the frogs.
workedExamples.answer: Both are elder-led, informal, mediation-based systems; Shimgelina adds five party-appointed elders with binding power, and jaarsummaa emphasises a win-win result.

workedExamples.problem: A woman's right has been violated in an Oromo community. Explain how the Siinqee institution responds.
workedExamples.given: Siinqee is a stick and an institution of Oromo women symbolising socially sanctioned rights; when a right is violated women ululate to notify one another and go to the Gada Council.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: an indigenous institution designed to protect rights and build peace.
workedExamples.substitution: The violated right triggers a collective response by women, who carry their Siinqee to the council and announce the wrongdoing in song.
workedExamples.calculation: Every woman is obliged to respond, the accused person is brought to justice before the council and appropriate punitive measures are taken, so the institution protects women's rights and restores peace.
workedExamples.answer: Women unite, carry their Siinqee to the Gada Council, announce the wrongdoing and secure justice for the violated right.

commonMistakes: Thinking indigenous conflict resolution is exactly the same thing as a formal court of law.
Believing elders are chosen at random rather than for their knowledge, maturity and practical experience.
Assuming formal courts are always better, when the textbook notes that the indigenous system is free from corruption and politicisation.
Confusing the Gadaa system with the rule of one person rather than a rotating democratic system of five classes.
Treating Siinqee as only a wooden stick and not as an institution that protects women's rights and builds peace.
Mixing up the peoples: Mada'a and Dagu belong to the Afar, not to the Oromo or the Amhara.
Forgetting that these mechanisms aim to restore relationships, not only to punish.
applications: Taking a family or neighbourhood dispute to respected elders before going to court, where local custom allows.
Recording the conflict resolution practices of your local elders as part of a school history project.
Using the Oromo proverb about the lake and the frogs in a class debate as an argument for win-win solutions.
Supporting women's rights institutions such as Siinqee and similar community groups.
Comparing the eight-year rotation of the Gadaa system with modern election cycles in a class discussion.
Settling a quarrel between two students by mediation rather than by immediate punishment.
g10-history-uh9-t2.summary: Ethiopia's indigenous knowledge appears in governance and dispute resolution systems that are informal, elder-led and based on local custom. They include the Mada'a and Dagu of the Afar, the Gadaa, jaarsummaa, gumaa and Siinqee of the Oromo, the Shimgelina of the Amhara, and the Luwa and Seera systems of the Sidama, Kambata and Hadiya. They work through arbitration and mediation, aim at solutions based on recognised customs and morality, and try to restore good relations; unlike formal justice systems they are described as free from corruption and politicisation.

g10-history-uh9-t3.overview: Heritage is what the past has passed to us, what we value in the present and what we choose to preserve for the future generation. This lesson defines heritage, distinguishes physical heritage from heritage practices, and explains the values that people place on heritage.
objectives: Define heritage and explain what it can include
Distinguish physical heritage objects from heritage practices
Explain what heritage values are
List the classifications of heritage values
Explain why heritage gives Ethiopians a sense of identity
g10-history-uh9-t3.simple: Heritage is something that can be passed from generation to generation, something that can be conserved or inherited and that has historic or cultural value. Our heritage is our inheritance: what the past has passed to us, what we value in the present and what we choose to preserve for the future generation. Heritage can be a physical object, such as a piece of property, a building or a place that can be owned and passed on. It also includes practices such as language, culture, popular song, literature and dress, which help us understand who we are. Heritage values are the meanings and values that individuals or groups give to heritage, including buildings, archaeological sites, landscapes and intangible traditions. These values may be historical, aesthetic, economic, social or scientific.
g10-history-uh9-t3.detailed:
What heritage means. Heritage is something that can be passed from generation to generation, something that can be conserved or inherited, and something that has historic or cultural value. Our heritage is our inheritance: what the past has passed to us, what we value in the present and what we choose to preserve for the future generation. Heritage includes everything that people want to save, including material culture and nature; it is the full range of our inherited traditions, monuments, objects and culture.

Heritage as physical objects and places. Heritage might be understood to be a physical object: a piece of property, a building or a place that can be owned and passed on to someone else. Our heritage includes those places with natural, indigenous or historic values that we have inherited and want to pass on to future generations.

Heritage practices. Besides these physical objects and places, there are also a variety of heritage practices that are preserved or passed down from generation to generation. Language, culture, popular song, literature and dress, for example, are just as significant in helping us comprehend who we are as the physical artifacts and buildings that we are more accustomed to thinking of as heritage. The unit introduction notes that intangible heritages, which include songs, recipes, languages and dances, attest to who we are and how we identify ourselves.

Heritage values. The term heritage values refers to the meanings and values that individuals or groups of people bestow on heritage, including buildings, archaeological sites, landscapes and intangible expressions of culture such as traditions. There are many classifications of values, including historical, aesthetic, economic, social, scientific and an array of other types.

Why heritage matters. Heritage provides an important context for our perception of ourselves as Ethiopians, and it is part of the social glue that binds communities together and expresses identity. Because heritage is both inherited and chosen, each generation decides what to conserve and what to pass on. When a community loses its language, its songs or its buildings, it loses part of the evidence of who it is.

Studying heritage as historians. Historians value heritage for the evidence it carries about the past. A building, an archaeological site, a manuscript or a ceremony can each be read as a source. The learning outcomes of this unit therefore ask students to differentiate tangible and intangible heritage and to respect others through exposure to a way of life different from their own.

keyTerms.def: Something that can be passed from generation to generation, can be conserved or inherited, and has historic or cultural value.
What the past has passed to us; heritage is described as our inheritance, what we value in the present and what we preserve for the future.
The physical objects made and used by people; heritage includes everything people want to save, including material culture and nature.
Practices such as language, culture, popular song, literature and dress that are preserved or passed down from generation to generation.
The meanings and values that individuals or groups of people bestow on heritage, including buildings, archaeological sites, landscapes and intangible expressions of culture.
One of the classifications of heritage value listed in the textbook, alongside aesthetic, economic, social and scientific values.
A people's sense of who they are; heritage expresses identity and is part of the social glue that binds communities together.

workedExamples.problem: A kebele committee must decide what to conserve. Using the definition of heritage, explain why a war memorial, a folk song and a river gorge can all be called heritage.
workedExamples.given: Heritage is something that can be passed from generation to generation, can be conserved or inherited, and has historic or cultural value; it includes places with natural, indigenous or historic values and also intangible practices such as language, song and dress.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: the definition of heritage as inherited historic or cultural value.
workedExamples.substitution: The memorial carries historic value, the folk song is a heritage practice, and the gorge is a place with natural value.
workedExamples.calculation: All three can be passed on, conserved and valued for historic, cultural or natural reasons, which is exactly what the definition requires.
workedExamples.answer: All three are heritage, because heritage includes physical objects and places, practices, and natural sites with inherited value.

workedExamples.problem: Two people disagree about an old building: one calls it valuable history, the other calls it only useful land. Which heritage values are in conflict?
workedExamples.given: Heritage values include historical, aesthetic, economic, social, scientific and other types, and heritage values are the meanings that individuals or groups bestow on heritage.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: classification of heritage values.
workedExamples.substitution: The first person appeals to historical and aesthetic value; the second appeals to economic value.
workedExamples.calculation: Both values are recognised classifications in the textbook, so the disagreement is not about truth but about which value is given priority.
workedExamples.answer: Historical and aesthetic value are being weighed against economic value, and the textbook recognises all of them.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why heritage is described as the social glue of Ethiopian communities.
workedExamples.given: Heritage provides an important context for our perception of ourselves as Ethiopians; the unit says intangible heritage attests to who we are and how we identify ourselves.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: the relationship between heritage and identity.
workedExamples.substitution: Shared monuments, languages, songs and ceremonies give people common reference points.
workedExamples.calculation: Common reference points create a shared sense of belonging, and that belonging is what binds communities together.
workedExamples.answer: Because it gives Ethiopians a shared sense of identity and belonging, heritage works as the social glue that binds communities together.

commonMistakes: Thinking heritage is only buildings and old objects.
Forgetting that language, songs, dress, recipes and literature can also be heritage.
Assuming heritage values are fixed and the same for everyone, when values are meanings that people bestow on heritage.
Believing heritage has no value if it cannot be sold.
Confusing one classification of heritage value, such as aesthetic value, with another, such as economic value.
Treating heritage as only about the past and forgetting that it is also what we choose to preserve for the future.

g10-history-uh9-t4.overview: Ethiopian heritage is divided into natural, tangible and intangible types, and many of the country's sites and traditions are registered by UNESCO. This lesson explains the three types and surveys Ethiopia's inscribed natural, tangible and intangible heritages.
objectives: Distinguish natural, tangible and intangible heritage
List the domains of intangible cultural heritage
Identify the Ethiopian heritages registered by UNESCO
Describe examples of Ethiopian monuments, temples, palaces, manuscripts and caves
Explain the historical value of sites such as Axum, Lalibela, Tiya and Harar Jugol
g10-history-uh9-t4.simple: Heritage has three main types: natural, tangible and intangible. Natural heritage consists of outstanding physical, biological, geological and natural formations and sites, valued for science, conservation or natural beauty. Intangible heritage is made up of practices, representations, expressions, knowledge, skills, instruments, objects and artefacts, shown in oral traditions, performing arts, social practices, rituals and festivals, knowledge of nature, and indigenous handicrafts. Tangible heritage is the physical artifacts produced, maintained and transmitted from generation to generation, such as buildings, monuments, artistic creations and historic places. Ethiopia has many UNESCO-registered heritages, including the Stelae of Axum, the Rock-hewn Churches of Lalibela, Fasil Ghebbi, the Simien Mountains, the Lower Valleys of Awash and Omo, Tiya, Harar Jugol and the Konso cultural landscape.
g10-history-uh9-t4.detailed:
Three types of heritage. There are different types of heritage: natural, tangible and intangible. Each type is preserved for future generations, and each can be found in Ethiopia. Festivals, for example, are classified under intangible heritage.

Natural heritage. Natural heritage consists of physical and biological formations, or groups of such formations, that are of outstanding value from the aesthetic or scientific point of view; geological and physiographical formations and precisely delineated areas that constitute the habitat of threatened species of animals and plants of outstanding value from the point of view of science or conservation; and natural sites or precisely delineated natural areas of outstanding value from the point of view of science, conservation or natural beauty.

Intangible heritage. Intangible heritage refers to those practices, representations, expressions, knowledge, skills, instruments, objects and artefacts. It is manifested in five domains: oral traditions and expressions, including language as a vehicle of the intangible cultural heritage; performing arts; social practices, rituals and festive events; knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universe; and indigenous handicrafts.

Tangible heritage. Tangible heritage refers to physical artifacts produced, maintained and transmitted from generation to generation. It includes artistic creations, buildings and historic places, monuments and artifacts that are considered worthy of preservation for the future.

Ethiopian heritages registered by UNESCO. The Stelae of Axum in Tigray symbolise the wealth and importance of the ancient Aksumite kingdom and were included in the List of World Heritage Sites in 1980. The Rock-hewn Churches of Lalibela in Amhara, eleven churches carved out of a single rock, were registered in 1978 and represent a unique artistic achievement in their execution, size and the boldness of their form. Fasil Ghebbi, the royal enclosure of King Fasiledes, stands in Gonder town. The Simien Mountains National Park in North Gondar is home to the Gelada baboon, the Simien fox and the Walia ibex and was one of the first sites included in the list in 1978. The Lower Valley of Awash, 300 km northeast of Addis Ababa in Afar Regional State, is a site of paleo-anthropological research listed in 1980. The Lower Valley of Omo in South Nations, Nationalities and Peoples Regional State was listed in 1980, and the discovery of many human and animal fossils and stone tools there has been of fundamental importance in the study of human evolution. Tiya, 90 km south of Addis Ababa in the Soddo Region, contains 36 monuments including 32 carved stelae covered with symbols and was listed in 1980. Harar Jugol is a fortified historic town 525 km from Addis Ababa whose wall was built during the time of Emir Nur Ibn Mujahid in the 16th century and which was registered in 2006. The Konso cultural landscape, an arid property of stone-walled terraces and fortified settlements in the Konso highlands, was inscribed in 2011.

Intangible heritages inscribed by UNESCO. Mesqel Demera, the ceremony of the Finding of the True Cross, was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013. Gadaa, the indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo people, was inscribed in 2016. Fichee-Chambalaalla, the Sidama New Year celebration and one of the most important Sidama holidays, was inscribed in 2015. Timket, the Ethiopian Epiphany that commemorates the baptism of Jesus in the Jordan River, is celebrated on 19 or 20 January and became Ethiopia's fourth entry on the UNESCO intangible cultural heritage lists in 2019. Ashenda, also called Ashendiye, Shadey or Solel, is the biggest and unique religious and cultural festival of Tigray and Amhara for girls and young women, and Irreecha, the annual Oromo thanksgiving celebrated at the beginning of Birra (spring) near water and trees, is held every September at Bishoftu Hora Harsadii and other Oromia cities.

Other tangible heritage: manuscripts, temples, mosques, palaces and caves. Ethiopia is exceptional in sub-Saharan Africa because it has a written tradition in the Ge'ez language, and after the introduction of Christianity in the 4th century manuscripts flourished with the support of the state; there were special schools of calligraphy in Gondar and Shewa, a school for bookbinding, and writing materials such as goatskin parchment, black and red inks from plants and minerals and pens made from local reed or bamboo. Among temples, the Temple of Yeha, located in Yeha northeast of Adwa, is a tower built in the Sabaean style and dated by comparison with ancient structures in South Arabia to around 700 BC. Other well-known monuments include the old cathedral of St. Mary of Zion at Aksum, rock-hewn churches and monasteries; mosques such as the Mosque of Negash in Tigray and the Grand Anwar Mosque in Addis Ababa; palaces such as the Palace of King Fasilidas, the Grand Palace of Menilek, the Palace of Jimma Abba Jifar II, the Palace of Ras Ali and the palace of Kumsa Moreda; the Sof Omar caves, one of the most remarkable and extensive underground cave systems in the world, formed by the Weyb River as it changed its course through limestone foothills; and the Halala Keela wall of Dawuro, dry-stone defences bordered by the Omo and Gojeb Rivers, begun probably in the second half of the 16th century and completed in the second half of the 18th century during the reign of King Halala.

keyTerms.def: Outstanding physical, biological, geological and physiographical formations and natural sites or areas valued from the point of view of science, conservation or natural beauty.
Physical artifacts produced, maintained and transmitted from generation to generation, such as buildings, historic places, monuments and artifacts.
Practices, representations, expressions, knowledge, skills, instruments, objects and artefacts, shown in five domains including oral traditions, performing arts, rituals and indigenous handicrafts.
A site inscribed on the UNESCO list because of its outstanding value, such as the Stelae of Axum, listed in 1980.
One domain of intangible heritage: spoken expressions, including language as a vehicle of the intangible cultural heritage.
One domain of intangible heritage, covering music, dance, drama and similar performances.
One of the five domains of intangible heritage listed in the textbook, covering locally made crafts.
A hand-written book or document; Ethiopia has a written tradition in the Ge'ez language and many manuscripts written on goatskin parchment.

workedExamples.problem: Classify each of the following as natural, tangible or intangible heritage: the Simien Mountains National Park, the Stelae of Axum, and Fichee-Chambalaalla.
workedExamples.given: Natural heritage is outstanding natural formations and sites; tangible heritage is physical artifacts such as monuments; intangible heritage is practices, expressions and festive events.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: the three types of heritage.
workedExamples.substitution: The park is a natural site that shelters threatened species; the stelae are carved monuments; Fichee-Chambalaalla is a New Year celebration.
workedExamples.calculation: Each item matches one type exactly: natural for the park, tangible for the stelae, intangible for the festival.
workedExamples.answer: The Simien Mountains National Park is natural heritage, the Stelae of Axum are tangible heritage and Fichee-Chambalaalla is intangible heritage.

workedExamples.problem: In which years were the Rock-hewn Churches of Lalibela, the Lower Valley of Awash and Harar Jugol registered by UNESCO, and what does the pattern show?
workedExamples.given: Lalibela was registered in 1978, the Lower Valley of Awash in 1980 and Harar Jugol in 2006.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: chronology of Ethiopia's World Heritage listings.
workedExamples.substitution: Place the dates in order on a timeline: 1978, then 1980, then 2006.
workedExamples.calculation: The first two listings fall close together at the end of the 1970s and the start of the 1980s, while Harar Jugol was added more than two decades later, so the pattern shows an early wave and later additions.
workedExamples.answer: 1978, 1980 and 2006 respectively; Ethiopia's first wave of World Heritage registration came in 1978 to 1980 and later sites such as Harar Jugol were added in 2006.

workedExamples.problem: Why is the Temple of Yeha important evidence for Ethiopian history?
workedExamples.given: The Temple of Yeha is located in Yeha, northeast of Adwa; it is a tower built in the Sabaean style and dated through comparison with ancient structures in South Arabia to around 700 BC.
workedExamples.formula: Historical framework: dating and style as evidence in history.
workedExamples.substitution: The building style links the tower to South Arabian architecture, and the comparison provides an approximate date.
workedExamples.calculation: A pre-Christian tower dated to about 700 BC shows connections between ancient Ethiopia and South Arabia, so the temple is evidence of long-distance cultural contact before Christianity.
workedExamples.answer: Because its Sabaean style, dated to around 700 BC, shows that ancient Ethiopia had cultural links with South Arabia long before Christianity.

commonMistakes: Calling a festival a tangible heritage; festivals are classified under intangible heritage.
Thinking natural heritage means only plants and animals, and not formations and sites valued for science, conservation or natural beauty.
Confusing tangible heritage, which is physical, with intangible heritage, which is expressed in practices, skills and expressions.
Mixing up the registration dates of Lalibela in 1978 and Harar Jugol in 2006.
Assuming that all Ethiopian heritage is registered by UNESCO, when only some sites and traditions are on the lists.
Forgetting that manuscripts and the Ge'ez written tradition are part of Ethiopia's tangible heritage.
applications: Making a class chart of local heritage sorted into natural, tangible and intangible.
Researching when each Ethiopian UNESCO site was inscribed and plotting the dates on a timeline.
Visiting a local monastery, mosque or palace and writing a description of its historical value.
Preparing a presentation on an intangible heritage such as Timket, Irreecha or Ashenda.
Photographing and describing a local natural site that deserves protection.
Writing to a local office to ask for better protection of a heritage site in your area.
g10-history-uh9-t4.summary: Heritage in Ethiopia falls into three types: natural, tangible and intangible. Natural heritage covers outstanding natural formations and sites; tangible heritage covers physical artifacts such as buildings, monuments and manuscripts; and intangible heritage covers practices, expressions, festivals and skills in five domains. Ethiopia has many UNESCO-registered heritages, from the Stelae of Axum and Lalibela, listed in 1980 and 1978, to Harar Jugol in 2006 and the Konso landscape in 2011, together with intangible entries such as Meskel in 2013, Fichee-Chambalaalla in 2015, Gadaa in 2016 and Timket in 2019.
